definition.text: The systematic grouping of soils by their distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how they are used.

facts.text: Classification systems group soils by measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed.
Soil science, engineering and environmental management all classify soils, to evaluate soil properties and decide on suitable land use.
Soil can be classified as a material, as geotechnical engineers do when judging foundations and building material, or as a resource.
Classification is old: inscriptions at the temple of Horus at Edfu record a soil classification used to choose temple sites, and ancient Greek scholars devised several.
Major modern systems include USDA soil taxonomy, the World Reference Base and engineering systems that judge soil stability and performance.
Standardized systems let soils be compared across regions and applications.
Knowledge of where soils occur has grown dramatically; SoilGrids maps soils worldwide at 1.00–0.25 km resolution from soil profiles and environmental data.
It remains a dynamic subject, with change in the structure of systems, the definitions of classes and their use in the field.

definition.text: The grouping of soils by the engineering properties that matter when they support foundations or serve as building material.

facts.text: Modern engineering systems are built to move easily from field observations to basic predictions of how a soil will behave.
The Unified Soil Classification System is the most common in North America; it and the fuller engineering description are standardized in ASTM D 2487.
Europe's ISO 14688 closely resembles the USCS but codes soils differently and adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.
In the United States the AASHTO system rates soils and aggregates for pavement construction, and the Modified Burmister system works like the USCS but codes more properties.
Moderately organic soils are treated as subdivisions of silts and clays, told apart by how their plasticity and Atterberg limits change on drying.
A full geotechnical description adds colour, in-situ moisture and strength, and more material detail than the USCS code carries.

definition.text: The contrast between natural systems, which group soils by intrinsic properties, behaviour or genesis, and technical systems, which group them by fitness for a particular use.

facts.text: Experience shows that natural classes, based on morphology, behaviour or genesis, can be interpreted for many different uses.
Some natural systems, such as the French Référentiel pédologique, rest on presumed soil genesis.
USDA soil taxonomy and the World Reference Base use morphology and laboratory tests as criteria for their hierarchical classes.
Differing ideas of pedogenesis, and of which morphological features matter for land use, shape each system's approach.
In U.S. soil survey, map units classed by soil taxonomy are also sorted into technical classes such as Land Capability Classes, hydric soil and prime farmland.
Numerical classification, or ordination, groups soil individuals by multivariate statistics such as cluster analysis, producing natural groupings without any inference about genesis.

definition.text: A U.S. workplace-safety scheme that sorts soils by strength so that excavations and trenches can be protected against collapse.

facts.text: It uses three soil types plus stable rock, based mainly on strength but also on other factors that affect the stability of cut slopes.

Type A soils are cohesive and plastic, with unconfined compressive strength above 1.5 tsf (144 kPa); Type B lie between 0.5 tsf (48 kPa) and 1.5 tsf; Type C fall below 0.5 tsf or are granular or seeping.
The lateral earth pressure each type induces rises from 25 psf per foot of depth for Type A to 45 for Type B and 80 for Type C.
Each type dictates how the excavation is cut or protected by sloping, shoring or shielding; the scheme guides construction safety, not the study of soil formation.

definition.text: A taxonomic unit of soil science: all soils that share a defined set of properties.

facts.text: In hierarchical systems soil types usually sit at a higher or intermediate level; they can be split into subtypes and combined into higher categories.
In the first U.S. classification (Whitney, 1909), by contrast, the soil type was the lowest level and the mapping unit.

Systems differ in what defines a type: German soil systematics uses mainly pedogenic features, WRB and USDA soil taxonomy add inherited parent-material traits, and the Australian Soil Classification ignores origin.
Horizons are a convenient basis, but some young soils lack clear horizons, so types may rest on whole-profile properties, as WRB defines Arenosols by sand content.
Many soils are shaped by human activity, and many systems define soil types to reflect it.
Because the term is so general, many systems avoid it: USDA soil taxonomy names six levels from order to series, and WRB calls its first level the Reference Soil Group.
In U.S. soil survey, 'soil type' was the original name of the soil phase, which records surface texture, slope, stoniness, saltiness and erosion.

definition.text: The soil classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the National Cooperative Soil Survey, which sorts soils by their properties into six levels from order to series.

facts.text: Its levels, from most general to most specific, are order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series.
The United States recognizes 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups, about 4,500 families and more than 14,000 series.
It uses quantitatively measurable properties: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content.
Guy Donald Smith, director of USDA soil survey investigations, originally developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural 1938 system.
Work began by 1945; a series of 'approximations' followed, the 7th in 1960, and the taxonomy appeared in 1975 with 10 orders and in 1999, revised, with 12.
It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide land use and soil management, and supplies the core criteria for U.S. soil map units.
Order names end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed.

definition.text: The second and third levels of USDA soil taxonomy: suborders split each order by properties tied to soil moisture and temperature, and great groups split suborders by the kind and sequence of horizons.

facts.text: Forty-seven suborders and about 185 great groups are recognized in the United States.
Great groups are told apart by horizons marked by clay, iron, humus or hardpans, and by features such as self-mixing shrink–swell clays, temperature and large amounts of salts.
Soil moisture regime names act as modifiers at the suborder level.
For example, the suborder Xeralfs contains the great group Durixeralfs, whose subgroup Abruptic Durixeralfs includes the San Joaquin series.

definition.text: The fourth level of USDA soil taxonomy, which divides each great group into typic, intergrade and extragrade subgroups.

facts.text: A typic subgroup carries the basic, typical concept of its great group.
An intergrade subgroup has properties grading toward another great group, suborder or order, but not expressed strongly enough to place it there.
Extragrade subgroups have aberrant properties that keep them out of any other class.
About 1,000 subgroups are defined in the United States.

definition.text: The fifth level of USDA soil taxonomy: a group of soils within a subgroup sharing the physical and chemical properties that govern their response to farming and engineering.

facts.text: Families are distinguished by texture, mineralogy, pH, permeability, structure, consistency, precipitation pattern and soil temperature, and sometimes by the percentages of silt, sand and coarse fragments.
About 4,500 families are recognized in the United States, and each may contain several soil series.
A family name stacks descriptors on the subgroup: 'fine-loamy, mixed, superactive, calcareous, Typic Torrifluvents' belongs to suborder Fluvents and includes the Jocity series.

definition.text: A class of soil temperature, set by mean annual and seasonal temperatures at 50 cm depth, used to classify soils in USDA soil taxonomy.

facts.text: Regimes such as frigid, mesic and thermic classify soils at lower levels, while the cryic regime separates some higher-level groups.
They rest on mean annual soil temperature, mean summer temperature and the summer–winter difference at 50 cm; mean annual soil temperature is normally taken as mean annual air temperature plus 2 °C.
Classes run from pergelic (about −8 to −4 °C) through subgelic, frigid (about 0 to 8 °C), mesic (8 to 15 °C) and thermic (15 to 22 °C) to hyperthermic (22 °C or higher).
Where mean summer and winter temperatures differ by less than 6 °C, the prefix 'iso' is added to the class name.

definition.text: A class describing how wet a soil stays through the year, defined by the groundwater table and the water available to plants.

facts.text: A soil's moisture regime, often reflecting climate, is a major control on the productivity of land ecosystems, farms included.
Moisture regime names modify soil names at the suborder level of USDA soil taxonomy.
Aquic soils are saturated and almost free of oxygen long enough to show gleying and mottling; they are common in wetlands.
Udic soils stay moist enough for plants year-round in most years and are common in humid regions.
Ustic soils lie between udic and aridic: moisture is usually available in the growing season, but severe droughts occur; they are common in semi-arid regions.
Aridic soils are dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days, as in deserts.
Xeric soils belong to Mediterranean-type climates, with cool, moist winters and long summer droughts.

definition.text: The earlier U.S. soil classification, which divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors.

facts.text: It grew from Curtis Marbut's scheme, begun in 1920, which became the 1935 system and, modified, was published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture, Soils and Men.
Zonal soils reflected climate and vegetation; intrazonal soils reflected a local factor of relief or parent material strong enough to override them.
At the top level soils were split into carbonate-rich pedocals of drier climates and pedalfers rich in aluminium and iron; 'alfer' later became the root of Alfisol.
It was a strictly natural system, and after 1938 classifying soil series under it met with mixed success; work on a replacement began by 1945.

definition.text: Soils whose profiles reflect a dominant local factor of relief or parent material more than the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

facts.text: Calcimorphic soils develop from limestone and include thin rendzinas, with limited available water, and deep red terra rossa soils of wetter climates.
Hydromorphic soils form in wetlands: gley soils, whose waterlogged, airless pores reduce iron and turn them grey-blue with red flecks, and peat soils, where plant remains never fully break down.
Halomorphic soils form through salinization.

definition.text: Immature soils that never get time to develop because their material keeps sliding downslope or is buried by fresh deposits.

facts.text: On mountain slopes such as the Himalayas, fine weathered material constantly slides downhill, leaving no time for soil to form.
On river flood plains new alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile.
Gleysols are called azonal soils that occur in nearly all climates, and Canada's system calls Anthroposols azonal soils highly modified or built by people.

title: Zonal soil

definition.text: In the 1938 U.S. system, the order of soils whose character reflects the regional climate and vegetation.

facts.text: Pedocals and pedalfers were both subdivisions of the zonal order.

Fertile, carbon-rich dark earths of North America and Eurasia were long explained as zonal soils of dry continental climates under steppe or prairie, before past human activity was recognized as a driver.

notes: No article or section of its own; passes the 2+ pages test (1938 USDA soil taxonomy, Pedocal, Pedalfer, Soil fertility).

title: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

definition.text: An international soil classification system for naming soils and building soil-map legends, edited by a working group of the International Union of Soil Sciences.

facts.text: It grew out of the FAO soil classification and the IUSS's International Reference Base project; its first edition appeared at the 1998 World Congress of Soil Science in Montpellier.
In 1998 the ISSS endorsed it as its correlation system and it replaced the FAO classification as the international system; USDA soil taxonomy also became a correlation system in 2014.
Further editions followed in 2006, 2014 (updated 2015) and 2022; the current fourth edition is open access under a Creative Commons licence.
It has two levels: 32 Reference Soil Groups, each refined by adding qualifiers, of which there are 202.
Classes rest mainly on soil morphology, from field and laboratory data, as an expression of pedogenesis; soil climate counts only as a soil-forming factor, not as a soil characteristic.
Its two levels resemble the French Référentiel pédologique, whereas USDA soil taxonomy is strongly hierarchical with six levels.
It is not meant to replace national systems, which may be more detailed for their own areas; the European Union uses it.
Group and qualifier names are capitalized and always given in English, so a soil carries the same name all over the world.

title: WRB diagnostics
article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#Architecture

definition.text: The diagnostic horizons, diagnostic properties and diagnostic materials on which the WRB bases its classification.

facts.text: Diagnostic horizons are typical products of soil formation with a minimum thickness, so they form a recognizable layer in the soil.
Diagnostic properties are typical results of soil-forming processes or reflect particular conditions of soil formation.
Diagnostic materials influence or indicate soil formation; they may be inherited from the parent material or produced by soil formation.
Each diagnostic has a name, such as argic horizon, stagnic properties or fluvic material.
Organic carbon sets one boundary: mineral material has less than 20% soil organic carbon, organic material 20% or more.
Diagnostic horizons entered the international system from the 1960 '7th approximation' of USDA soil taxonomy, by way of the FAO legend.
Only the diagnostic criteria decide whether a diagnostic is present in a soil.

title: Naming a soil with the WRB
article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#Naming a soil

definition.text: The WRB procedure that keys a soil out to a Reference Soil Group and then adds every qualifier that applies to it.

facts.text: The key asks, in a fixed sequence, whether given diagnostics occur in given depth ranges, plus traits such as clay content; the soil goes to the first group whose criteria it meets.
Principal qualifiers precede the group name, the highest-ranked closest to it, with Haplic used if none applies; supplementary qualifiers follow in brackets.
Specifiers such as Epi- (0 to 50 cm) and Endo- (below 50 cm) turn qualifiers into depth-related subqualifiers, such as Epiarenic.
In the worked example, a loess soil with clay migration becomes an Amphialbic Endostagnic Luvisol, followed by supplementary qualifiers such as Anosiltic, Endoloamic and Aric.

title: WRB map legends
article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#Creating map legends with the WRB

definition.text: The WRB rules for naming the units of a soil map, where the number of qualifiers used depends on the map's scale.

facts.text: Three map scale levels use the Reference Soil Group alone, the group plus its first applying principal qualifier, or the group plus the first two.
A map unit names an association of soils: dominant soils cover at least 50%, codominant 25 to 50% and associated 5 to 25%; smaller shares are ignored.
Matching scale levels to actual map scales is difficult because the choice depends on how uniform the landscape is.
Only the third and later editions can build map legends; the second edition could only name soils.

title: Reference Soil Groups
article: World Reference Base for Soil Resources#List of the Reference Soil Groups according to WRB 2022

definition.text: The 32 top-level classes of the World Reference Base, each with a two-letter code, listed in the order of its key.

facts.text: The key opens with Histosols, with thick organic layers, then soils under strong human influence: long and intensively farmed Anthrosols and artefact-rich Technosols.
Groups that limit root growth are Cryosols (permafrost), Leptosols (thin or stony), Solonetz (sodium-rich clayey subsoil), Vertisols (shrink–swell clays) and Solonchaks (soluble salts).
Groups set apart by iron and aluminium chemistry are Gleysols, Andosols, Podzols, Plinthosols, Planosols, Stagnosols, Nitisols and Ferralsols.
Chernozems, Kastanozems, Phaeozems and Umbrisols have organic-rich mineral topsoils; Durisols, Gypsisols and Calcisols accumulate secondary silica, gypsum or carbonates.
Clay-enriched subsoils mark Retisols and four groups split by clay activity and by whether exchangeable aluminium exceeds base cations: Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols.
The key ends with little-differentiated soils: Cambisols (moderately developed), Fluvisols (stratified sediments), Arenosols (very sandy) and Regosols (no significant development).
Group names are plural in map legends and singular everywhere else.

definition.text: A supra-national soil classification developed by the FAO, generalizing how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors.

facts.text: It began as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO Soil Map of the World, published 1971–1981 in 10 volumes at 1:5 million; Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend.
It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'.
Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with soil phases, three texture classes and three slope classes.
Simple and broad, it was the first truly international system, fitting most soils from field descriptions, and meant for continental rather than local maps.
The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings and underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database.
United Nations projects applied it and many countries adapted it; many of its names are known widely with similar meanings.
The World Reference Base replaced it in 1998.
In the 1974 legend, Leptosols on calcareous rock were called Rendzinas and those on acid rock Rankers.

definition.text: The general-purpose, hierarchical system currently used to describe and classify soils in Australia.

facts.text: It has five levels, from most general to most specific: order, suborder, great group, subgroup and family.
Ray Isbell, a retired CSIRO soil scientist, developed it and first published it in 1996; later editions came in 2002, 2010 and March 2021.
It superseded the Factual Key (1960) and the Handbook of Australian Soils (1968); since Isbell's death in 2001 the National Committee on Soil and Terrain has led its updates.
Its fifteen orders run from Anthroposols, Arenosols and Calcarosols to Sodosols, Tenosols and Vertosols, many reflecting the arid, strongly weathered Australian continent.
In seven orders, suborders name the dominant colour of the upper B2 horizon (Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey or Black), giving names such as Red Kurosol.
Other orders have their own suborders: Hydrosols, for instance, split into Intertidal, Supratidal, Salic, Redoxic and other Hydrosols.
It defines soil types without asking whether their properties result from soil formation.
Some equivalents: Histosols are Organosols, and Podzols are Podosols.

definition.text: Canada's national soil classification, closer to the U.S. system than any other but designed to cover only Canadian soils.

facts.text: Introduced in 1955, it was designed to separate soils formed by pedogenic processes in cool climates; earlier Canadian work had used U.S.-like systems.
Its five levels are order, great group, subgroup, family and series: it drops the suborder, and separates Solonetzic and Gleysolic soils at order level.
Ten orders sit at the top; 31 great groups subdivide them by properties reflecting differences in soil-forming processes.
Its unit is the pedon, a 3-dimensional body commonly 1 metre across and 1 to 2 metres deep, classified with a key using horizon thickness, Munsell colour and pH.
Subgroups follow horizon sequence and often intergrade to other orders; families add parent material and soil climate, as in 'Orthic Gray Luvisol, clayey, mixed, cold, subhumid'.
A series name such as Breton implies all the properties of its order, great group, subgroup and family, supporting many judgements of land suitability.
Class limits are arbitrary, since nature has few sharp breaks in the soil continuum, and the system changes as mapping and research add knowledge.
Recent research proposes adding a Leptosolic order for soils that are shallow or over bedrock.

title: Cryosolic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Cryosolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils with permafrost within 1 metre of the surface, or 2 metres if strongly churned by frost.

facts.text: Because permafrost blocks roots and water, the seasonally thawed active layer above it can turn saturated and semifluid in spring.
Disturbing the boreal forest or tundra cover melts ground ice, which can make soil slump and disrupt roads, pipelines and buildings.
Cryosolic soils cover about 3,672,000 km2 (about 40%) of Canada and dominate much of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.
Defined in 1973 after Mackenzie Valley surveys, the order has three great groups: Turbic Cryosols, mixed by cryoturbation; Static Cryosols, on sandy or gravelly material; and peaty Organic Cryosols.

title: Canadian Organic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Organic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils made mostly of organic matter, over 30% by weight in the upper half metre, without permafrost near the surface.

facts.text: They are the main soils of peatlands such as swamps, bogs and fens, mostly built from plants of waterlogged ground, though some come from lake deposits or forest litter on rainy, rocky slopes.
Organic soils cover almost 374,000 km2 (4.1%) of Canada, with large areas in Manitoba, Ontario and northern Alberta.

Four great groups follow decomposition: little-decomposed soils with over 40% fibre, mostly from Sphagnum, as Fibrisols; others with 10–40% or up to 10% fibre; and thick forest-litter soils over rock.

title: Vertisolic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Vertisolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of clay-rich soils that shrink and swell markedly as they dry and wet.

facts.text: Shrinking and swelling cut shiny slickensides in the subsoil, mix former surface material downward and prevent or scramble subsurface horizons.
They form mainly in clayey materials of the semiarid to subhumid Interior Plains and cover less than 1% of Canada.
Recognized in the 1990s after studies of Great Plains pedons, the order has two great groups, Vertisol and Humic Vertisol, told apart by the darkness of the A horizon.

title: Podzolic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Podzolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of acid soils whose B horizon accumulates amorphous humified organic matter bound to aluminium and iron.

facts.text: They form mostly in sandy materials under forest or shrubs in cold, humid climates.
Percolating water leaches bases; organic acids from litter free iron and aluminium, and the complexes become insoluble and settle in the B horizon once metals reach a critical proportion.
Podzolic soils occupy 14.3% of Canada, in the Appalachian Uplands and Canadian Shield and in British Columbia, usually under coniferous forest.
Great groups follow the B horizon: Humic Podzols are low in iron, Ferro-Humic Podzols hold at least 5% organic carbon, and Humo-Ferric Podzols, the commonest, less than 5%.

title: Gleysolic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Gleysolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils that are periodically or permanently saturated with water and depleted of oxygen.

facts.text: When flooding comes with soil warmer than about 5 °C, microbes use up the oxygen within days and nitrate and ferric oxide are reduced.
Losing ferric oxide turns the soil grey; when it dries, reoxidized iron forms yellow-brown mottles, so poor drainage and drab grey colour identify these soils.
Gleysolic soils cover about 117,000 km2 (1.3%) of Canada, in depressions and level areas of subhumid and humid climates.
Its three great groups are Humic Gleysols, with a dark organic A horizon, Gleysols without one, and Luvic Gleysols, with a clay-enriched B horizon.

title: Solonetzic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Solonetzic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils whose B horizon is very hard when dry and swells into a sticky, compact mass when wet, because of sodium.

facts.text: They usually develop in saline parent materials in semiarid and subhumid regions.
Sodium ions make the clay disperse and swell on wetting, closing large pores and stopping water flow.
Solonetzic soils cover almost 73,000 km2 (0.7%) of Canada, mostly in southern Alberta.
As leaching moves salts and sodium downward, soils develop from saline parent material to Solonetz, Solodized Solonetz and Solod; resalinization can reverse this.

title: Chernozemic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Chernozemic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of grassland soils whose A horizon is darkened by organic matter, mostly from decaying grass roots.

facts.text: The A horizon is neutral to slightly acid and rich in bases such as calcium; the C horizon usually holds lime and may hold gypsum.
With mean annual soil temperatures above 0 °C, they cover more than 4% of Canada and dominate the grassy southern Interior Plains.
Four great groups follow surface colour and dryness: Brown soils in the driest areas, Dark Brown, thick-topped Black soils under tall grass, and transitional Dark Gray soils.

title: Luvisolic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Luvisolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of soils with a leached Ae horizon above a Bt horizon in which the washed-down clay has been deposited.

facts.text: They typically form under forest in subhumid to humid climates where the parent material holds appreciable clay; in saline or calcareous material, salts and carbonates leach before the clay moves.
Luvisolic soils cover about 809,000 km2 (8.8%) of Canada, largely in the central to northern Interior Plains.
Two great groups split by soil temperature: Gray Brown Luvisols, at 8 °C or more, in the Great Lakes–St Lawrence Lowlands, and Gray Luvisols of the boreal Interior Plains.

title: Brunisolic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Brunisolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order for soils with developed B horizons that meet the requirements of none of the other orders.

facts.text: Many have brownish B horizons without the clay build-up of Luvisolic soils or the amorphous material of Podzolic soils, and some evolve into one or the other.
Brunisolic soils cover almost 790,000 km2 (8.6%) of Canada, in all regions south of the permafrost zone.
Four great groups follow the A horizon and acidity: Melanic Brunisols have an Ah at least 10 cm thick and pH above 5.5, Sombric a thick Ah below pH 5.5; Eutric and Dystric lack a thick Ah.

title: Regosolic order
article: Canadian system of soil classification#Regosolic Order

definition.text: The Canadian order of weakly developed soils whose properties are essentially those of their parent material.

facts.text: They support plants but have not been stable long enough to develop well-differentiated horizons.
The name joins Greek rhēgos, 'blanket', with Latin solum, 'soil'; Regosolic soils cover about 0.8% of Canada.
Two great groups are defined: Regosols, made essentially of C horizons, and Humic Regosols, with an Ah horizon at least 10 cm thick.

definition.text: The system used to describe, classify and organize knowledge about the soils of Poland.

facts.text: The Soil Science Society of Poland published editions in 1956, 1959, 1974, 1989, 2011 and 2019; early ones followed Dokuchaev's natural criteria, the 2011 edition quantitatively defined diagnostic horizons, materials and properties.
Each soil is described three ways: its type, from genesis and diagnostic horizons; its kind, the geological origin of the bedrock; and its texture class.
Soil type is the basic unit, and types are grouped into orders by the presence or absence of diagnostic horizons and properties.
It borrows much from USDA soil taxonomy (1999) and the WRB (2006) and gives equivalents: its rusty soils, sandy soils with rusty horizons, match WRB Arenosols and USDA Psamments.

title: Référentiel pédologique

definition.text: The French soil reference system, a natural classification based on presumed soil genesis.

facts.text: Like the WRB, it has two hierarchical levels; versions appeared in 1992, 1995 and 2008.
Its reference soil types, relevant to European soils, carry names such as Brunisol, Calcarisol, Colluviosol, Fluviosol, Podzosol and Reductisol, refined by terms such as humic or typic.

definition.text: An American highway-engineering system that classifies soils and soil–aggregate mixtures for road construction.

facts.text: Hogentogler and Terzaghi first developed it in 1929, and it has been revised several times since.
Soils with 35% or less passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve are granular materials; those with more than 35% are silt–clay materials.
Groups run from A-1 to A-7, set by sieve results and by the liquid limit and plasticity index of the fraction passing 0.425 mm (No. 40).
As road subgrade, granular materials rate excellent to good and silt–clay materials fair to poor.

definition.text: The lowest level of USDA soil taxonomy, grouping pedons with similar pedogenesis, soil chemistry and physical properties.

facts.text: A series groups pedons whose horizons match in colour, texture, structure, pH, consistency, composition and arrangement in the profile, so the soils perform alike for land use.
The concept dates from 1903, when series were meant as soils alike in origin, from the same kind of rock or sediment, but differing in texture.
Series are named after a town or landmark near where they were first recognized, such as Haugan, Montana, though a series such as Hagerstown can range across several states.
More than 14,000 series are recognized in the United States; they are the most homogeneous classes in the taxonomy.
A series may be a taxonomic unit, the conceptual core of a class, or a mapping unit outlining similar soils on the land; the two need not fully coincide.
Map units carry the name of their dominant series: in Greenbrier County, West Virginia, unit LhE is 80% Lily series, the rest Dekalb, Berks and less stony soils.

conflicts.text: Soil in the United States says over 20,000 soil series have been identified in the United States.
conflicts.note: USDA soil taxonomy (S:f68ea89e7370) says more than 14,000; both are lower bounds, probably from different dates.

definition.text: A soil that a U.S. state has chosen as having special significance to it.

facts.text: Every state has selected one, and twenty have been established by law, giving them the same standing as official state flowers and birds.
Representative soils have also been chosen for Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
Examples include San Joaquin in California (1997), Drummer in Illinois (2001) and Port Silt Loam in Oklahoma (1987).
The Cecil soil, which runs from Virginia to Alabama, is the state soil of North Carolina.

definition.text: The soils in which grapevines grow, whose make-up is one of the most important considerations in planting a vineyard.

facts.text: Soil anchors the vine's roots and governs drainage and the minerals and nutrients the vine receives.
The ideal is thin topsoil and subsoil that hold enough water yet drain well, so roots are not waterlogged; soil that stores or reflects heat also affects ripening.
Growers name soils by rock or texture: limestone-based Kimmeridgian soil is the principal type of the Loire Valley, Champagne and Burgundy.
Sandy soils drain well but hold water poorly, and the phylloxera louse does not thrive in them.

definition.text: A soil developed over non-calcareous material, usually rock.

facts.text: It is often called an A/C soil, because its topsoil, the A horizon, sits directly on unaltered parent material, the C horizon.
Some classifications group it as lithomorphic, together with the rendzina, the similar soil over calcareous material.
In the 1974 FAO legend, Leptosols on acid rock were called Rankers and those on calcareous rock Rendzinas.
Polish Soil Classification keeps Rankers as a type of weakly developed soil, matched to WRB Regosols and USDA Udorthents and Udifolists.

definition.text: A soil moisture regime in which water is present but limited at times when conditions suit plant growth, intermediate between aridic and udic.

facts.text: The name comes from Latin ustus, 'burnt'; the regime is common in semi-arid and sub-humid climates.
Averaged over the year, stored moisture plus rainfall is less than the water lost by evapotranspiration.
Ustic soils suit drought-tolerant crops; maize there generally needs supplemental irrigation, which udic soils do not require.
The long dry season gives a wide harvest window: farmers in Brazil's Cerrado harvest grain at a leisurely pace.

definition.text: In the 1938 U.S. classification, a major group of soils rich in aluminium and iron, in which sesquioxides increase relative to silica as the soil forms.

facts.text: Pedalfers were a subdivision of the zonal order; together with the carbonate-rich pedocals they formed the top level of Marbut's classification.
They began at about the udic border, and lateritic soils were one of their three subdivisions.
The term is no longer used in U.S. soil classification but survives in college geology texts, and its 'alf' lives on in the name Alfisol.

definition.text: A soil series of the Wisconsin Till Plains that is the state soil of Indiana.

facts.text: It formed in up to 18 inches (46 cm) of loess or silty material over calcareous loamy till, under native hardwood forest.
Some 794,994 acres (3,217 km2) are mapped in Indiana; the fertile, gently sloping soils grow corn, soybeans and winter wheat and help rank the state in farm output.
USDA soil taxonomy classifies it as fine-loamy, mixed, active, mesic Oxyaquic Hapludalfs, an Alfisol.
It is an old series: by 1906 the Miami series already held 16 soil types from glaciated regions.

definition.text: A soil profoundly modified or constructed by people, with one or more natural horizons altered, removed or replaced.

facts.text: Anthroposols occur on industrial, commercial, urban and resource-extraction sites and along transport, fuel and power corridors.
Human-made soils were long left out of classification systems because criteria built for natural soils often do not apply to them.
A proposed Canadian order requires a disturbed D horizon at least 10 cm thick or removed natural horizons, with great groups set by artefacts or organic carbon; ordinary tillage does not qualify.
The WRB splits such soils into Anthrosols, long cultivated, and Technosols, holding industrial products and artefacts; Australia's system also has an Anthroposol order.

title: Argillic

definition.text: The USDA soil taxonomy term for a subsurface horizon enriched in clay.

facts.text: Clay accumulates mainly by illuviation, the downward washing of existing clay, with some clay formed in place.
It is a diagnostic subsurface horizon used to define higher categories: Alfisols and Ultisols require it, Histosols and Entisols never have it, and other orders vary.
An argillic horizon needs at least 1.2 times the clay of any overlying eluvial horizon and usually shows clay films or bridges visible by eye or hand lens.
A 2014 study by James Bockheim found argillic horizons in 44% of U.S. soil series.
It is the starting point for kandic horizons, dominated by low-CEC 1:1 clays, and natric horizons, rich in exchangeable sodium; fragipans commonly form within it.
The WRB equivalent is the argic horizon, from the same Latin root argilla; it needs at least 8% clay and a texture class other than sand.
Buried paleo-argillic horizons, as in the Wounded Moose paleosol of the Yukon, show that the climate was once hot and wet enough to form them.

notes: Argillic gives argilla as 'clay' in the lead (S:bd4d58e03846) and as 'white clay' in the WRB section (S:8050db0c64fc).

definition.text: An earlier soil classification system developed for Australian soils.

facts.text: First published in 1968, it built on the great soil group classification that J. A. Prescott published in 1931.
The Australian Soil Classification has since superseded it, as it did the 1960 Factual Key.

definition.text: A soil group of the FAO soil classification, named from English 'grey' and Russian zemlja, 'earth'.

facts.text: The name refers to uncoated silt and quartz grains in its organic-rich layers; it forms in decalcified loose deposits such as wind-blown, river and lake sediments and glacial till.
With Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems it forms a set of steppe and prairie soils with a mollic horizon, where organic matter accumulates faster than leaching removes it.
One of the original 26 FAO groups, it remained among the 28 of the 1988 revision, with two units: gleyic and haplic greyzems.
It correlates most closely with Dark Grey Chernozems in Canada and with Albolls and Boralfic Boroll subgroups in USDA soil taxonomy.

conflicts.text: Greyzem says the FAO system was introduced with the UNESCO Soil Map of the World in 1978.
conflicts.note: FAO soil classification (S:de4d98df6761) and WRB (S:6062235a8bd5) date the map's legend, the FAO classification, to 1974.

definition.text: The soil moisture regime of humid climates, where stored moisture plus rainfall roughly equals or exceeds evapotranspiration.

facts.text: Water moves down through the soil at some time in most years.
In USDA soil taxonomy, udic soils are moist enough year-round in most years to meet plant needs; the ustic regime lies between udic and aridic.
Suborders such as udalfs (Alfisols), udepts (Inceptisols) and udolls (Mollisols) have a udic moisture regime.

title: Kurosol

definition.text: One of the fifteen soil orders of the Australian Soil Classification: soils with a sharp texture contrast between a lighter surface and a strongly acidic, clay-rich subsoil.

facts.text: What sets kurosols apart from other texture-contrast orders is the upper B horizon: strongly acidic in kurosols, sodic in sodosols, and neither in chromosols.
The strongly acidic subsoil generally has a pH below 5.5 measured in water.
They are widespread in higher-rainfall, strongly leached and weathered landscapes of eastern and southern Australia.
The dense clay subsoil and acidity can restrict roots and water and cause aluminium and manganese toxicity; lime corrects surface acidity, but deep acidity is hard to fix.

notes: Assigned to this chapter by the concept graph; it would sit more naturally beside the Australian Soil Classification (classification-systems).

definition.text: The international standard that sets basic principles for identifying and classifying soils for engineering purposes.

facts.text: ISO 14688-1 covers natural soils in situ, similar man-made materials in situ and soils redeposited by people.
It grades clay as particles smaller than 2 μm, and sand as fine, medium and coarse with limits at 0.063, 0.2, 0.63 and 2.0 mm.
Gravel is graded fine, medium and coarse with limits at 2, 6.3, 20 and 63 mm.
It closely resembles the Unified Soil Classification System but codes soils differently and adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

definition.text: The soil moisture regime typical of Mediterranean climates, with cool, moist winters and warm, dry summers.

facts.text: Like the ustic regime, it has long summer droughts.
It names suborders: Xerolls are Mollisols and Xeralfs Alfisols of Mediterranean climates.
Greek red soils fall partly in Rhodoxeralfs, Palexeralfs and Xerochrepts, xeric Alfisols and Inceptisols.

definition.text: The soil moisture regime of arid and semi-arid climates, in which soil is dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days.

facts.text: Its control section, at 50 cm depth, is judged against soil temperatures above 5 °C and 8 °C in counting dry and moist days.
Aridisols must have an aridic moisture regime.
It is also called torric: Torripsamments are Psamments with an aridic or torric regime.
The ustic regime is wetter than the aridic and drier than the udic.

definition.text: A soil moisture regime in which the soil is saturated long enough each year to be virtually free of dissolved oxygen.

facts.text: A soil must be saturated for at least a few days a year to count as aquic.
Aquerts are Vertisols with aquic conditions for some time in most years and redoximorphic features; high clay slows permeability, favouring such conditions.
Many Histosols show aquic conditions or artificial drainage.
